chapter.name: Diversity in the Living World
chapter.blurb: The great variety of plants and animals observed on a nature walk; grouping plants by height and stem into herbs, shrubs, trees, climbers and creepers; grouping by leaf venation, root type and cotyledon number into monocots and dicots; grouping animals by their movement and body parts; and how habitats shape the adaptations, biodiversity and conservation of plants and animals.

scope_in.item: Record and compare features of different plants (stem hardness/thickness, leaf shape/arrangement, flower colour/shape/scent) observed on a nature walk
Record and compare features of different animals (habitat, food, movement) observed on a nature walk

Explain that the variety of plants and animals found in a region is called biodiversity, and that members of a region's biodiversity depend on each other, e.g. trees give birds food and shelter, animals spread seeds
Group plants into herbs, shrubs and trees based on height, stem thickness/hardness/colour and where branching starts, using examples like tomato, rose and mango
Identify climbers (weak stems needing support) and creepers (stems that creep along the ground)
Identify reticulate venation (net-like veins on both sides of a thick middle vein, e.g. hibiscus) and parallel venation (veins running parallel, e.g. banana, grass) in leaves
Identify taproot (one main root with small side roots, e.g. mustard, hibiscus) and fibrous root (bunch of similar thin roots, e.g. grass) systems
State the general relation between leaf venation and root type: reticulate venation with taproots (e.g. sadabahar, chickpea), parallel venation with fibrous roots (e.g. lemongrass, wheat)

Distinguish dicotyledons (two cotyledons, e.g. chickpea) from monocotyledons (one cotyledon, e.g. maize), and relate cotyledon number to venation and root type (dicots: reticulate venation + taproot; monocots: parallel venation + fibrous root)
Group animals by the type of movement (fly, run, crawl, walk, hop, jump) and the body part used (legs, wings, fins), using examples such as ant, goat, pigeon, housefly and fish
Explain, using fish and goats as examples, that an animal's body parts for movement suit its surroundings - a streamlined body and fins for water, legs for land

Define adaptation as the special features that let a plant or animal survive in its region, using examples: fleshy desert-plant stems that store water; conical, sloping-branched deodar trees that shed snow; hot-desert camels' long legs, wide hooves, single hump and low water loss; cold-desert (Ladakh) camels' two humps, shorter legs and long hair; and rhododendrons that are shorter with smaller leaves on windy mountaintops but taller elsewhere

Define habitat as the place where a plant or animal lives that provides its food, water, air and shelter; classify habitats as terrestrial (land, e.g. forests, deserts, grasslands, mountains) or aquatic (water, e.g. ponds, lakes, rivers, oceans); define amphibians as animals like frogs that live in both

Explain that damage to habitats causes loss of homes, food and resources and so leads to loss of biodiversity, citing the Bengal Tiger, Cheetah and Great Indian Bustard as examples, and name Project Tiger (1973) and the Cheetah Reintroduction Project (2022) as conservation measures
Describe sacred groves as undisturbed, community-protected patches of forest found across India that shelter many plants (including medicinal ones) and animals

scope_out.reason: Not mentioned anywhere in this chapter

scope_out.item: Food chains, food webs, or producer/consumer/decomposer roles
scope_out.reason: The chapter mentions interdependence only anecdotally (trees feeding birds, animals spreading seeds, p. 14), without introducing formal food-chain concepts

scope_out.item: Camouflage or protective colouration as a type of adaptation
scope_out.reason: All the adaptation examples given (desert plants, deodar, camels, rhododendrons) are about surviving temperature, water scarcity, wind or snow, never about hiding from predators

scope_out.reason: Only herb/shrub/tree/climber/creeper and monocot/dicot groupings are used in this chapter

scope_out.reason: The Bengal Tiger, Cheetah and Great Indian Bustard are named only as examples of habitat loss and conservation projects; no formal endangerment categories are introduced

scope_out.reason: The chapter uses only plain region names such as desert, mountain, terrestrial and aquatic, never technical adaptation-type terms

concepts.name: Diversity in plants and animals around us
concepts.description: The variety of plants and animals observed around us, recorded by their features, and how this variety and their interdependence make up a region's biodiversity.
concepts.idea: The plants and animals around us show great variety in their features, and this variety is called biodiversity.
concepts.rule: On a nature walk, students record the features of plants in Table 2.1 - the hardness/thickness of the stem, the shape and arrangement of leaves, and the colour, shape and scent of flowers - and the features of animals in Table 2.2 - where they live, the food they eat, and how they move. Observing this variety shows that plants and animals have many different features. The variety of plants and animals found in a particular region contributes to the biodiversity of that region. Each member of a region's biodiversity has a different role to play: trees provide food and shelter to birds and other animals, and animals help spread seeds after eating fruits. This shows that plants and animals in a region are dependent on each other.
concepts.example: A crow lives in a tree, eats insects, and moves by flying and walking; a mango tree provides shelter to birds - showing how the different plants and animals around us, and their interdependence, add up to biodiversity.

questions.q: Compare the kind of information recorded about plants in Table 2.1 with the kind of information recorded about animals in Table 2.2, and explain why different kinds of features are used for the two groups.
questions.a: For plants, features such as stem hardness, leaf shape/arrangement and flower colour/shape/scent are recorded because plants stay rooted in one place and are best distinguished by their structure; for animals, features such as habitat, food and movement are recorded because animals move around and interact with their surroundings, so these behavioural features better distinguish them.

questions.q: Do you agree that simply counting the number of plants and animals in a park tells you everything about its biodiversity? Give a reason.
questions.a: No, biodiversity is about the variety of different kinds of plants and animals, not just their total number; a park with a hundred trees of the same kind has less biodiversity than a park with ten different kinds of plants and animals.

questions.q: Design a simple two-column observation sheet, like Table 2.1 or 2.2, that a student could use on a nature walk to compare three plants and three animals, listing the kinds of features you would record for each group and why.
questions.a: For plants, record features such as stem (hard/soft, thick/thin), leaves (shape/arrangement) and flowers (colour/shape/scent), because these structural features best show plant variety; for animals, record features such as habitat, food eaten and way of moving, because these behavioural features best show animal variety; recording both sets of features for three plants and three animals would reveal the biodiversity of the area.

concepts.name: Grouping plants by height and stem: herbs, shrubs, trees, climbers and creepers
concepts.description: Grouping plants into herbs, shrubs, trees, climbers and creepers based on their height and the thickness, hardness and branching pattern of their stems.
concepts.idea: Plants can be grouped as herbs, shrubs or trees based on their height and the thickness/hardness of their stem and where branching starts; climbers and creepers are grouped by their weak stems.
concepts.rule: Some plants grow very tall and have hard, thick, brown, woody stems whose branches typically start higher up on the stem, away from the ground; these are called trees, for example a mango tree. Some plants are not as tall as trees; they have hard, brown, woody stems that are not as thick, and branch very close to the ground; these are called shrubs, for example a rose plant. Some plants are small with soft, green stems; these are called herbs, for example a tomato plant. Some plants have weak stems that need support to climb and grow, and are called climbers; some plants creep along the ground and are called creepers. Table 2.3 records the height, nature of the stem, and where branches appear, to help group plants this way.
concepts.example: A rose plant, with hard woody stems that branch close to the ground, is a shrub, while a tomato plant, with a soft green stem, is a herb.

concepts.name: Leaf venation, root types and cotyledons
concepts.description: Grouping plants by leaf venation (reticulate/parallel), root type (taproot/fibrous) and the number of cotyledons in their seeds (dicot/monocot), and the general relationship among these three features.
concepts.idea: Leaves show reticulate or parallel venation, roots are taproot or fibrous, and seeds have one or two cotyledons (monocot/dicot); these three features are generally linked.
concepts.rule: The pattern of veins on a leaf is called venation. In reticulate venation, veins form a net-like pattern on both sides of a thick middle vein, as in hibiscus leaves. In parallel venation, veins run parallel to each other, as in banana and grass leaves. Roots also show two types: a taproot has one main root with small side roots arising from it, as in mustard and hibiscus; a fibrous root system is a bunch of similar-sized thin roots arising from the base of the stem, as in common grass. Seeds also differ: a chickpea seed splits into two parts, each called a cotyledon, so chickpea is a dicotyledon (dicot); maize has a single thin cotyledon, so it is a monocotyledon (monocot). Generally, plants with reticulate venation have taproots (e.g. sadabahar, chickpea/chana), while plants with parallel venation have fibrous roots (e.g. lemongrass, wheat); dicot plants generally have reticulate venation and taproots, while monocot plants generally have parallel venation and fibrous roots.
concepts.example: Wheat, a monocot, has parallel venation in its leaves and fibrous roots, while chickpea, a dicot, has reticulate venation and a taproot.

concepts.name: Grouping animals by movement
concepts.description: Grouping animals by the type of movement they perform and the body parts, such as legs, wings and fins, that they use to move.
concepts.idea: Animals can be grouped by how they move and which body parts they use to move, such as legs, wings or fins.
concepts.rule: Table 2.5 records different animals, their type of movement, and the body parts used for it: an ant uses legs; a goat walks and jumps using legs; a pigeon walks and flies using legs and wings; a housefly walks and flies using legs and wings; a fish swims using fins. Different animals have different types of movement - they can fly, run, crawl, walk, hop or jump - and they use different body parts to do so, such as wings, legs and fins. Grouping animals based on their movement and the body parts used helps identify similarities and differences among them and is important for understanding animal diversity. A fish has a streamlined body and fins suited to moving in water, while a goat moves with the help of legs suited to moving on grassy land.
concepts.example: A pigeon uses its legs to walk and its wings to fly, while a fish uses its fins to swim - different body parts suited to different types of movement.

concepts.name: Adaptations and habitats: terrestrial, aquatic and amphibians
concepts.description: How the special features of plants and animals, called adaptations, suit them to their habitat, and how habitats are grouped as terrestrial, aquatic, or both (amphibians).
concepts.idea: The special features that help a plant or animal survive in its surroundings are called adaptations, and the place where it lives is called its habitat; habitats can be terrestrial, aquatic, or both (amphibians).
concepts.rule: A fish has a streamlined body and fins for movement in water; a goat lives in grassy areas and moves with legs. Cactus plants in the hot desert have thick, fleshy stems that store water and help them tolerate hot conditions. Deodar trees in cold mountains are conical with sloping branches, letting snow slide off easily. Camels of the hot desert have long legs and wide hooves to avoid sinking in sand, one hump to store food, and excrete very little urine, produce dry dung and do not sweat much, so they lose very little water and can survive many days without drinking. Camels of the cold desert of Ladakh have two humps (which shrink in winter as stored food is used), shorter legs suited to mountains, and long hair for warmth. Rhododendrons in the windy Shola forests of the Nilgiris are shorter with smaller leaves to survive heavy winds on mountain tops, while in Sikkim they grow taller. These special survival features are called adaptations. The place where a plant or animal lives, which provides its food, water, air and shelter, is called its habitat. Habitats where plants and animals live on land are terrestrial habitats (forests, deserts, grasslands, mountains); habitats in water are aquatic habitats (ponds, lakes, rivers, oceans). Animals such as frogs that live in water as well as on land are called amphibians.
concepts.example: A camel of the hot desert has long legs and wide hooves to avoid sinking in the sand and one hump to store food, while a camel of the cold desert of Ladakh has two humps, shorter legs and longer hair - both are adaptations to survive their different desert habitats.

questions.a: Its two humps store food that it uses when food is scarce in winter, and its long hair from head to neck helps it survive the cold winters of Ladakh.

questions.q: Rhododendrons in the Nilgiris are shorter with smaller leaves, while those in Sikkim are taller. Explain why the same kind of plant can look different in different mountain regions.
questions.a: In the windy Shola forests of the Nilgiris, rhododendrons are shorter with smaller leaves to survive the heavy winds on mountain tops, while in Sikkim's milder conditions, they can grow taller; this shows adaptations can vary even within the same species depending on the exact conditions of the region.

questions.a: The hot-desert camel has one hump for storing food and long legs with wide hooves to avoid sinking in sand, suited to a hot, sandy desert; the Ladakh camel has two humps that shrink and are used for food in winter, shorter legs suited to mountainous terrain, and long hair that protects it from the cold, all suited to a cold, mountainous desert.

questions.q: Explain why the biodiversity of a hot desert differs from the biodiversity of a snowy mountain, using the adaptations of plants and animals found in each region.
questions.a: A hot desert has very little water and is hot by day and cold by night, so it has plants like cactus with water-storing fleshy stems and animals like the hot-desert camel with wide hooves and low water loss; a snowy mountain has frequent snowfall and cold conditions, so it has plants like the deodar tree, whose conical, sloping shape sheds snow, and animals adapted to the cold; because the two regions have very different conditions, the plants and animals adapted to survive there, and hence the biodiversity, are also very different.

questions.q: A friend says that an animal's habitat and its adaptations have nothing to do with each other. Do you agree? Give a reason using an example from the chapter.
questions.a: No, an animal's adaptations are the special features that let it survive in its particular habitat; for example, a fish's streamlined body and fins are adaptations suited specifically to its aquatic habitat, showing the two are closely connected.

questions.q: Imagine a new animal that lives in a very windy, cold mountain habitat. Design three adaptations it could have to survive there, explaining how each feature would help, using the deodar tree and rhododendron as inspiration.
questions.a: It could have a compact, low body shape (like the shorter rhododendron) to resist strong winds; a sloped or streamlined outer covering (like the deodar's conical shape) to let snow slide off rather than pile up; and thick fur or hair (like the Ladakh camel) to protect it from the cold, each feature matching a specific challenge of a windy, cold, snowy mountain habitat.

concepts.name: Habitat loss and protecting biodiversity
concepts.description: How habitat damage causes loss of biodiversity, and how India protects plants and animals through conservation projects and community-protected sacred groves.
concepts.idea: Damage to habitats causes loss of biodiversity, and India protects its plants and animals through conservation projects and community-protected sacred groves.
concepts.rule: When the habitat of plants and animals is damaged, they lose their homes, food and other resources, which leads to loss of biodiversity. The populations of the Bengal Tiger, Cheetah and Great Indian Bustard have declined in India due to loss of natural habitats caused by human activities. Project Tiger was initiated in 1973 to protect the declining population of the Bengal Tiger. The Cheetah Reintroduction Project was initiated in 2022 to restore the Cheetah's population. Habitats of the Great Indian Bustard have been declared Protected Areas in Gujarat, Rajasthan and Maharashtra. The Save Silent Valley Movement is a real success story from the Palakkad district of Kerala, where common people campaigned for about ten years, using awareness programmes, letters to editors, newspaper articles, seminars and petitions, against a proposed hydroelectric dam, and succeeded in saving the forest's rich biodiversity. Sacred groves are undisturbed patches of forest, found all over India, protected by local communities who do not allow anyone to harm animals, cut trees, or disturb the area; they are home to many kinds of plants (including medicinal plants) and animals, making them a community-protected treasure of biodiversity. We must protect biodiversity to ensure our planet stays full of life.
concepts.example: Project Tiger, started in 1973, was launched to protect the declining population of the Bengal Tiger caused by loss of its natural habitat.

questions.q: Using the examples of the Bengal Tiger, the Cheetah and the Great Indian Bustard, explain how habitat loss threatens biodiversity and describe one conservation measure taken for each.
questions.a: The Bengal Tiger's population declined due to loss of its natural habitat, and Project Tiger was started in 1973 to protect it; the Cheetah had declined similarly, and the Cheetah Reintroduction Project was initiated in 2022 to restore its population; the Great Indian Bustard's habitat loss led to its habitats being declared Protected Areas in Gujarat, Rajasthan and Maharashtra; together these show that habitat loss reduces biodiversity, and each species needed its own conservation measure to recover.

questions.q: Compare government-led conservation efforts, such as Project Tiger, with community-led protection, such as sacred groves, in how each helps protect biodiversity.
questions.a: Project Tiger is a government initiative that declares and manages Protected Areas or reserves specifically to save a declining species like the Bengal Tiger; sacred groves are patches of forest protected informally by local communities out of tradition, without government management; yet both approaches prevent the loss of habitat, whether formally through a designated project or informally through community respect for the forest, and so both help preserve biodiversity.
s: Comparison of how each protects biodiversity

questions.q: Do you think community efforts like sacred groves are as important as government projects like Project Tiger for protecting biodiversity? Give a reason.
questions.a: Yes, because sacred groves show that ordinary communities, without government orders, can successfully protect forests and their biodiversity over generations, just as government projects like Project Tiger protect declining species through official measures; both approaches contribute to conservation.

questions.q: Design a simple class project, like the ones suggested at the end of the chapter, to help protect biodiversity in your own school or neighbourhood, and explain how each part of your project would help.
questions.a: The project could include: (1) planting and labelling native trees in the school garden, which restores habitat for local birds and insects; (2) creating a small 'no-disturbance' corner similar to a sacred grove, which lets a patch of ground develop its own plant and animal life undisturbed; and (3) preparing a presentation about local conservation projects like Project Tiger to spread awareness, which encourages more people to protect biodiversity.
